name: The Grand Canyon
scope: The Colorado River's mile-deep gorge across northern Arizona. T1: it runs ~277 miles (446 km) long and over a mile (>1,800 m) deep -- a single river cut this. T1: the striped walls stack like a book, each colored band a different vanished world (beach, reef, desert dune). T2: the pale Coconino Sandstone band is fossilized desert dunes -- a Sahara frozen into stone a mile up. T2: the rim's Kaibab Limestone was a shallow SEA floor -- sea-shell fossils sit a mile ABOVE the river. T3: the Colorado only began carving the canyon ~5-6 million years ago -- startlingly recent for such deep rock (invert: ancient walls, young cut). T3: the dark rock at the very bottom (the Vishnu basement schist) is ~1.7-1.8 BILLION years old. T4: the Great Unconformity -- at one contact ~1.2 billion years of rock is simply MISSING between two touching layers. T4: Havasu Creek's blue-green travertine waterfalls at Supai, where the Havasupai still live -- the most remote community in the lower US, mail still delivered by mule. T5: the canyon keeps deepening because the whole Colorado Plateau slowly rises while the river saws down. T5: John Wesley Powell's one-armed 1869 crew made the first descent through the then-unmapped rapids. (deep: ~12 rungs, 2-3 per tier.)
source: Grokipedia 'Grand Canyon'; NPS grca 'Vishnu Basement Rocks' & 'Missing Time / Great Unconformity'; USGS Geology of Grand Canyon NP; AMNH 'Building the Canyon's Layers'; Wikipedia 'Grand Canyon', 'Havasupai'.
framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER, lead with the scene ('a river that cut a mile down'), never 'What is the largest canyon?'. Accuracy rail: the basement rocks are ~1.7-1.8 Gyr (Vishnu Schist 1.74 Gyr; Elves Chasm pluton 1.84 Gyr) -- the seed's '2 billion' is a round figure, use the real numbers; the Great Unconformity gap is ~1.2 Gyr (525-Ma Tapeats resting on 1.74-Gyr schist). Dinner-test payoff: the Havasupai-at-Supai / mail-by-mule rung and the 'sea-shells a mile above the river' rung. Distractors: other great canyons/rivers (Yarlung Tsangpo, Copper Canyon, Colca) keep all four live. Lane border: answers stay PLACE/earth-process facts, not a mineral's chemistry.
history_overlap: The Powell-1869 rung could touch a history-bank exploration episode; keep its answer the PLACE-fact (first descent of the canyon) and drop the rung if the history bank already owns Powell.

name: Yellowstone
scope: The world's first national park, sitting on a supervolcano in Wyoming. T1: Old Faithful erupts a boiling column ~30-55 m high on a schedule -- about every 90 minutes (hook: a geyser you can set a watch by). T1: the Grand Prismatic Spring glows in rings of blue, green, yellow, orange and red. T2: those colors are living heat-loving microbes (thermophiles) -- each ring a different temperature; the orange/red pigments act as the microbes' sunscreen. T2: Yellowstone holds ~500 geysers -- more than HALF of all the geysers on Earth. T3: the whole park sits inside a caldera ~30 by 45 miles -- the collapsed crater of a supervolcano. T3: Steamboat Geyser is the world's TALLEST active geyser, firing up to ~120 m, but on no schedule at all. T3: Mammoth Hot Springs builds a white terraced staircase of travertine as spring water drops its dissolved limestone. T4: the volcano has erupted catastrophically at least three times (2.1M, 1.3M, 640,000 years ago); the caldera floor still rises and falls as magma shifts. T4: the hotspot stays fixed while North America slides southwest over it, leaving a trail of dead calderas across Idaho's Snake River Plain. T5: a heat-loving microbe from a Yellowstone hot spring (Thermus aquaticus) gave the world the enzyme behind PCR DNA testing -- a discovery born in this water. T5: the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone drops the Lower Falls past cliffs stained yellow by hydrothermal alteration. (deep: ~12 rungs, 2-3 per tier.)
source: NPS 'Old Faithful Geyser', yell 'Volcano'; USGS YVO 'Old Faithful' & 'Grand Prismatic'; Wikipedia 'Yellowstone Caldera', 'Grand Prismatic Spring', 'Steamboat Geyser', 'Thermus aquaticus'; NASA Earth Observatory 'Grand Prismatic'.
framing_note: Voice: invert the wonder -- the superlative ('half the world's geysers', 'tallest active geyser') is the HOOK, the named place/feature is the answer; never 'What is a geyser?' (teach the term first). Accuracy rail: Grand Prismatic is the largest hot spring in the US / third-largest in the world; Old Faithful's interval varies 50-127 min (avg ~90) -- don't state a fixed clock. Dinner-test payoff: the Thermus aquaticus->PCR rung and Steamboat-as-tallest. Lane border: the thermophile-color and PCR rungs stay PLACE facts ('a discovery from this spring', 'microbes color the water') -- the microbe's own biology belongs to the science/animal banks, so keep the answer about the SPRING.

name: Uluru & Kata Tjuta
scope: A single giant red rock rising from the flat heart of the Australian desert. T1: Uluru stands 348 m high (863 m above sea level) -- an island of stone on an empty plain. T1: it appears to glow deep red at sunrise and sunset. T2: the red is rust -- a thin skin of iron oxide on the sandstone; break the surface and the rock inside is grey. T2: it's an inselberg -- an 'island mountain' left standing after millions of years eroded the softer land around it (teach the term). T3: most of Uluru is underground -- the visible rock is the tip of a far larger slab whose layers dip and continue deep below (exact extent unknown). T3: the sandstone layers, once flat lake-and-fan sediment ~550 Ma, were tilted almost VERTICAL -- the strata stand on end. T4: nearby Kata Tjuta (the Olgas) is actually TALLER (546 m) but made of a different rock -- conglomerate, a natural cement of boulders and pebbles. T4: rare desert rains turn the rock into cascading waterfalls and fill hidden waterholes and painted caves at its base. T5: Uluru is sacred to the Anangu (Pitjantjatjara and Yankunytjatjara); after decades of their requests, climbing it was permanently banned in October 2019. T5: Uluru and Kata Tjuta are outcrops of the SAME buried rock mass -- twin tips of one underground formation. (deep: ~10 rungs.)
source: Grokipedia 'Uluru'; Wikipedia 'Uluru', 'Kata Tjuta'; IUGS Geoheritage 'Uluru inselberg'; Britannica 'Uluru/Ayers Rock'; Parks Australia (climbing ban Oct 2019).
framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER; lead with the glowing-red scene, not 'What is the largest monolith?' (it is NOT the world's largest -- avoid that false superlative). Accuracy rail: do NOT claim a specific underground depth ('5-6 km' is a myth) -- say the strata dip and extend far below by an unknown amount; the arkose is tilted near-vertical. Dinner-test payoff: 'the rock is literally rusting' and the near-vertical strata. vision_mandated TRUE: this is an indigenous-sacred place -- name the Anangu as custodians, present the 2019 climbing ban respectfully as their long-sought decision, active voice. Lane border: geography owns the rock and desert, never a desert animal's biology.

name: Cappadocia
scope: A moonscape of soft-rock cones in central Turkey, hollowed out by hand. T1: the valleys bristle with 'fairy chimneys' -- tall stone cones, many wearing a boulder like a hat. T1: whole villages of homes and churches are carved straight INTO the rock. T2: the rock is tuff -- volcanic ash from ancient eruptions of Mt Erciyes and Mt Hasan, hardened into soft, carvable stone. T2: each chimney's 'hat' is a harder basalt cap that shields the soft tuff beneath from rain -- so the sheltered column survives while the rest erodes away. T3: at Goreme, medieval monks cut churches into the cliffs and covered the cave walls with Byzantine frescoes still glowing today. T3: beneath the fields lies Derinkuyu -- an entire underground city carved 18 levels deep, ~85 m down. T4: Derinkuyu could shelter around 20,000 people plus their livestock, with stables, wells, and even wineries underground. T4: giant rolling millstone doors sealed the tunnels from the INSIDE, locking out invaders. T5: air shafts and wells kept the deepest levels breathable and watered, and tunnels reportedly linked Derinkuyu to other buried cities kilometres away. T5: today balloonists drift over the chimneys at dawn -- the same soft rock, seen from above. (deep: ~11 rungs.)
source: Smithsonian 'Turkey's Fairy Chimneys'; MuchBetterAdventures 'How Cappadocia's Fairy Chimneys & Underground Cities Formed'; Atlas Obscura 'Derinkuyu'; UNESCO WHS 'Goreme NP and Rock Sites of Cappadocia'; Wikipedia 'Derinkuyu', 'Cappadocia'.
framing_note: Voice: lead with the carved-cone scene; teach 'tuff' before testing it. Accuracy rail: fairy chimneys form because a hard cap protects soft tuff (differential erosion) -- don't say wind 'blew' them into shape; Derinkuyu is 18 levels / ~85 m / ~20,000 people. Dinner-test payoff: the rolling-stone doors and the '20,000 people in a buried city' rung. Lane border: a one-line mention of an underground winery is fine, but this is NOT a food-origin ladder (that's the cooking bank).
history_overlap: The early-Christian-refuge angle at Derinkuyu could touch a history episode -- keep answers the PLACE/engineering fact (the rolling doors, the depth, the capacity), not a dated raid narrative.

name: Giant's Causeway & Fingal's Cave
scope: A pavement of stone columns marching into the sea in Northern Ireland. T1: it's made of ~40,000 basalt columns packed tight, most of them perfect six-sided hexagons -- like a giant's paving. T2: the columns formed as a thick sheet of lava cooled and shrank, cracking into pillars from the top down (teach: columnar jointing). T2: not all are hexagons -- some have 5, 7 or 8 sides; hexagons just pack most neatly. T3: the lava erupted ~60 million years ago as the North Atlantic was tearing open. T3: legend says the giant Finn McCool (Fionn mac Cumhaill) built the causeway to stride across to Scotland. T4: the SAME lava flow surfaces across the sea at Fingal's Cave on the Scottish isle of Staffa -- identical columns, the 'other end' of the giant's road. T4: named shapes dot the site -- the Giant's Boot, the Organ, the Chimney Stacks. T5: Fingal's Cave so moved composer Felix Mendelssohn that he wrote 'The Hebrides' overture -- a wonder that became music. (standard: ~8 rungs.)
source: Wikipedia 'Giant's Causeway', 'Fingal's Cave'; UNESCO WHS 369; British Geological Survey 'The Giant's Causeway and Causeway Coast'; NTS Staffa geology; Britannica 'Giant's Causeway'.
framing_note: Voice: lead with the '40,000 fitted hexagons' scene, then reveal the cooling-lava mechanism; the legend and the geology are BOTH true wonders -- hold them side by side (label the Finn McCool story as legend). Accuracy rail: columns are mostly but not all hexagonal; Fingal's Cave (Staffa) is the same ~60-Ma flow. Dinner-test payoff: the Mendelssohn 'Hebrides Overture' rung (a cultural creation born of the place). Distractors: other basalt-column sites (Devils Postpile, Svartifoss) keep choices live.

name: Salar de Uyuni
scope: The world's largest salt flat, high on the Bolivian Altiplano. T1: it stretches 10,582 km2 of blinding white salt, flat to the horizon. T1: when a thin film of rain covers it, it becomes the world's largest MIRROR -- sky and ground merge into one. T2: the dry salt crust cracks into endless repeating hexagon tiles. T2: it is the flattest large surface on Earth -- so flat that satellites are calibrated against it. T3: beneath the crust lies brine holding a huge share of the world's lithium -- the metal in every phone and EV battery. T3: it's the dried bed of a vanished Ice-Age lake (Lake Tauca) that evaporated away, leaving the salt behind. T4: Incahuasi 'Island' rises from the white sea, bristling with giant cacti centuries old. T4: it's an endorheic basin -- rivers flow IN but none flow out, so every mineral they carry stays and concentrates (teach the term). T5: the salt is metres thick in places and still forms as brine wicks up and evaporates in the thin, dry mountain air. (standard: ~8 rungs.)
source: Wikipedia 'Salar de Uyuni'; NASA Earth Observatory 'Lithium Harvesting at Salar de Uyuni'; Live Science 'Salar de Uyuni'; USGS/GESAMP lithium-resource figures (Bolivia ~22% of world resources, 2024).
framing_note: Voice: invert the wonder -- the size/mirror is the hook, the knowable fact (largest salt flat, calibration-flat surface, lithium store) is the answer; never 'What is the largest salt flat?'. Accuracy rail: 10,582 km2; it holds a large SHARE of world lithium RESOURCES (Bolivia ~a fifth+), not 'most of the world's lithium mined'. Dinner-test payoff: the mirror rung and the cactus-island rung. Lane border: the giant cacti are scenery -- answer the PLACE-fact ('an island of ancient cacti in a sea of salt'), not the cactus's botany.

name: Ha Long Bay
scope: A drowned forest of limestone towers off northern Vietnam. T1: more than 1,600 steep limestone islands rise straight out of an emerald-green sea. T2: 'Ha Long' means 'descending dragon' -- legend says dragons sent to defend Vietnam spat jewels and jade that fell into the sea and became these islands, walling out invaders. T3: they are tower karst -- limestone slowly dissolved by rain into steep pinnacles, then partly drowned as the sea rose (teach: karst). T3: the towers reach up to ~400 m; the bay is one of the New7Wonders of Nature. T4: hidden inside the towers are vast caves like Sung Sot ('Surprise Cave'), cathedral-sized chambers hung with stalactites. T5: some islands hide a lagoon in their heart -- a ring of cliff around still water reachable only by paddling through a low sea-cave tunnel. (standard: ~6 rungs.)
source: Wikipedia 'Ha Long Bay'; UNESCO WHS 672 + IUCN Technical Evaluation; NASA Earth Observatory 'The Emerald Isles of Ha Long Bay'.
framing_note: Voice: lead with the 'towers rising from the sea' scene; teach 'karst' before testing it. Accuracy rail: ~1,600 tower-karst limestone islands, up to ~400 m, drowned by post-Ice-Age sea rise; label the descending-dragon story as legend (and the source of the name). Dinner-test payoff: the hidden-lagoon-inside-an-island rung and Sung Sot cave. Lane border: the bay's langurs/wildlife are an animal aside -- keep answers the PLACE/karst fact.

name: Bryce Canyon
scope: A hillside of stone spires in southern Utah. T1: it's packed with hoodoos -- thin, tottering rock towers -- the densest crowd of them anywhere on Earth. T2: it isn't really a canyon at all: no river cut it. It's a set of natural amphitheatres eaten BACKWARD into the edge of a high plateau (teach the difference). T2: the rock is the pink Claron limestone; iron gives it its rose and orange glow. T3: the sculptor is frost -- water freezes in cracks more than 200 nights a year, prying the rock apart bit by bit (teach: frost wedging). T3: each hoodoo is capped by a harder stone that shelters the softer rock below into a totem-pole shape. T4: to the Paiute the hoodoos are the Legend People (To-when-an-ung-wa), turned to stone by the trickster Coyote for their misdeeds. T5: Bryce sits at the very top of the Grand Staircase -- a giant flight of cliffs whose lowest step, far to the south, is the Grand Canyon. (standard: ~7 rungs.)
source: NPS 'Bryce Canyon: Hoodoos Cast Their Spell'; Wildland Trekking 'Hoodoos of Bryce'; BryceCanyonCountry 'Native American Lore'; Wikipedia 'Bryce Canyon National Park', 'Grand Staircase'.
framing_note: Voice: lead with the spire-forest scene; the payoff is the surprise that it's NOT a river canyon. Accuracy rail: hoodoos are carved by frost wedging + rain, not wind; the caprock/soft-rock contrast makes the totem-pole shape. Dinner-test payoff: the Paiute 'Legend People turned to stone' rung and the Grand-Staircase-to-Grand-Canyon link. Distractors: other hoodoo/spire sites (Cappadocia's chimneys, Cathedral Gorge) keep choices live.

name: Pamukkale & Hierapolis
scope: A white cliff of stone terraces in southwestern Turkey. T1: from a distance it looks like a frozen cotton-white waterfall of pools -- its name means 'cotton castle'. T2: the white rock is travertine -- limestone left behind as hot spring water cools and its dissolved lime hardens (teach the term). T2: the pools are warm mineral water you can wade in, stepping down the terraces. T3: the terraces keep GROWING -- as long as the springs flow, fresh white rock forms; greying pools are re-flooded to stay bright. T3: an entire ancient Greco-Roman spa city, Hierapolis, sits on top of the white cliff. T4: at Cleopatra's Pool you swim among fallen marble columns of a temple an earthquake toppled into the water. T4: Hierapolis's Ploutonion -- 'Pluto's Gate' -- was a cave breathing invisible toxic CO2; priests called it a doorway to the underworld, and birds that flew in dropped dead at its mouth. T5: the springs are geothermally heated groundwater rich in calcium carbonate -- the same recipe as a stalactite, but building open-air terraces. (standard: ~7 rungs.)
source: Wikipedia 'Pamukkale'; UNESCO WHS 485 'Hierapolis-Pamukkale'; Live Science 'Pamukkale: Turkey's cotton castle'; NASA Earth Observatory 'Turkey's Cotton Castle'; reporting on 2013 Ploutonion rediscovery.
framing_note: Voice: lead with the 'cotton castle' scene; teach 'travertine' before testing it. Accuracy rail: travertine is deposited by cooling calcium-carbonate-rich spring water (CO2 degasses, lime precipitates) -- not 'salt', not snow. Dinner-test payoff: the Ploutonion / 'Pluto's Gate' death-cave rung (real: rediscovered 2013, confirming ancient accounts) and the submerged-marble Cleopatra's Pool. Lane border: Hierapolis is a place/culture fact -- no history-episode duplication intended.

name: Mount Roraima
scope: A sheer-walled table mountain rising like an island above the South American jungle. T1: it's a tepui -- a flat-topped mountain with vertical cliff sides, standing alone above the rainforest (teach the term). T2: its 2,810 m summit marks the triple border where Venezuela, Brazil and Guyana meet. T2: the top is almost always wrapped in cloud -- a hidden world above the weather. T3: its sandstone is ~1.7-2 billion years old -- among the OLDEST exposed sedimentary rock on Earth. T3: cut off on its cliff-top island for millions of years, Roraima grew plants and animals found nowhere else on the planet. T4: waterfalls pour straight off the summit's rim; the flat top is a maze of black rock, pools and pale 'quartz gardens'. T5: Roraima's inaccessible plateau inspired Arthur Conan Doyle's 1912 novel 'The Lost World', where dinosaurs survive atop a tepui. (standard: ~7 rungs.)
source: Grokipedia 'Mount Roraima'; Wikipedia 'Mount Roraima', 'The Lost World (Conan Doyle novel)'; Beautiful World Travel Guide 'Mount Roraima'; geology references on the Roraima Group sandstone.
framing_note: Voice: lead with the island-above-the-jungle scene; teach 'tepui' before testing it. Accuracy rail: Angel Falls is on a DIFFERENT tepui (Auyan-tepui) -- do NOT attribute it to Roraima; Roraima's own runoff makes cliff-edge falls. Dinner-test payoff: the 'Lost World' rung (a book born of the place). Lane border: the endemic-life rung stays a PLACE-fact about ISOLATION ('life found nowhere else because the summit is an island') -- a specific creature's biology belongs to the animal bank.

name: Devil's Tower
scope: A lone stone tower rising sheer from the plains of Wyoming. T1: it climbs 867 ft (265 m) straight up, its sides ribbed with enormous vertical columns. T2: it's the hard core of magma that cooled UNDERGROUND; the softer rock around it eroded away, leaving the tower standing (teach: igneous intrusion). T2: the ribs are giant columns of phonolite that cracked as the magma cooled and shrank -- the same physics as the Giant's Causeway, super-sized. T3: in 1906 it became the very FIRST national monument in the United States, declared by Theodore Roosevelt. T4: to the Lakota and Kiowa it is Bear Lodge (Mato Thipila): children fleeing a giant bear were lifted skyward on rising rock, and the bear's claws raked the sides into the columns we see. T5: the tower starred as the aliens' landing site in the 1977 film 'Close Encounters of the Third Kind', making its shape famous worldwide. (standard: ~6 rungs.)
source: Wikipedia 'Devils Tower'; NPS Geodiversity Atlas 'Devils Tower NM'; USGS 'Devils Tower NM'; Rock & Gem 'Devils Tower: Geology and Legends'; IUGS Geoheritage 'Devils Tower, Mateo Tepe'.
framing_note: Voice: lead with the lone-tower scene; the payoff is that the 'tower' is the exhumed guts of a cooled intrusion. Accuracy rail: the exact origin (laccolith / volcanic neck / intrusion) is still DEBATED -- say 'magma cooled underground, then the soft rock eroded away'; present BOTH names (Devils Tower and Bear Lodge) and note the 1875 'Devils Tower' name is a disputed mistranslation many tribes want changed. Dinner-test payoff: the Bear Lodge bear-claw legend and the Close Encounters rung. Distractors: other columnar/intrusion landmarks keep choices live.

name: Zhangye Danxia (Rainbow Mountains)
scope: Hills striped in rainbow bands in Gansu, China. T1: the mountainsides are painted in stripes of red, orange, yellow, green and blue-grey, like a layer cake tipped on its side. T2: the red is rust -- iron oxide staining the sandstone; other trace minerals tint the other bands. T3: the stripes are layers of sand and mud laid down flat, one atop another, over the age of the dinosaurs (Cretaceous). T4: the whole flat layer-cake was TILTED onto its edge by the same tectonic collision that raised the Himalayas -- which is why we see the bands side-on. T5: this red-bed, cliff-and-tower landform has a name, 'Danxia'; Zhangye is its most colourful example and a UNESCO Global Geopark. (standard: ~5 rungs.)
source: Wikipedia 'Zhangye National Geopark'; China Highlights 'Zhangye Danxia'; Forbes/Trevor Nace 'Rainbow Mountains of China'; UNESCO Global Geopark listing.
framing_note: Voice: lead with the painted-hills scene; each rung a different fact (color -> cause -> layering -> tilting -> the named landform), no theory-stacking. Accuracy rail: colors come from iron oxide + trace minerals in sedimentary layers (real geology), NOT dye or algae; the tilt is Himalayan-orogeny tectonics. Dinner-test payoff: the 'flat layers tilted on edge by the Himalaya collision' rung. Distractors: other colorful rock sites (Vinicunca/Peru's Rainbow Mountain, Arizona's Painted Desert) keep choices live.

name: Dallol & the Danakil Depression
scope: An alien landscape of acid pools in the Afar desert of Ethiopia. T1: neon-green and sulphur-yellow pools bubble and steam across a crust of salt -- one of the most other-worldly places on Earth. T2: it sits in the Danakil Depression, ~120 m BELOW sea level, and ranks among the hottest inhabited places on the planet. T3: the pools are hydrothermal -- groundwater heated by shallow magma, so loaded with salt, iron and sulphur that some are as acid as battery acid (near pH 0) (teach: hydrothermal). T3: the colors are minerals -- iron and sulphur crusting the ground green, yellow and orange. T4: this is where three tectonic plates pull APART -- Africa is slowly tearing open here, and one day the sea will flood in to make a new ocean (teach: rift). T5: nearby Erta Ale cradles a permanent lava lake -- one of only a handful on Earth whose molten surface never cools. (standard: ~6 rungs.)
source: Wikipedia 'Dallol (hydrothermal system)', 'Danakil Depression', 'Erta Ale'; PMC 'The Dallol Geothermal Area ... Planetary Field Analog'; All That's Interesting 'Inside Dallol'.
framing_note: Voice: lead with the acid-pool 'another planet' scene; teach 'hydrothermal' and 'rift' before testing them. Accuracy rail: Danakil is ~120 m below sea level; Dallol's pools are hyperacidic (near pH 0) and hydrothermal, colored by iron/sulphur; the Afar is a three-plate rift junction. Dinner-test payoff: 'a continent is tearing apart here' and the Erta Ale permanent lava lake. Lane border: keep answers PLACE/earth-process facts; extremophile microbes living in the pools are a science/biology aside, not the answer.

name: Chocolate Hills of Bohol
scope: A field of near-identical green cones on Bohol island, the Philippines. T1: more than 1,200 (about 1,268) rounded conical hills dot the plain, so alike they look built to a pattern. T2: in the dry season the grass covering them browns off and the whole field turns chocolate-brown -- which is how they got their name. T3: they're karst -- limestone uplifted from an old sea floor, then dissolved by rain into these cones (teach: karst); local legend credits two feuding giants who hurled sand and stone until they made peace. (mini: ~3 rungs.)
source: Wikipedia 'Chocolate Hills'; UNESCO Global Geopark 'Bohol Island'; GeologyScience 'Chocolate Hills Philippines'.
framing_note: Voice: lead with the 'a thousand identical hills' scene; the name-payoff (they turn chocolate-brown in the dry season) is the dinner-test rung. Accuracy rail: ~1,268 cone-karst LIMESTONE hills; the brown is dried grass, not the rock's color. Lane border: Bohol's tarsier is an animal aside -- keep every answer the PLACE/landform fact.

name: Wave Rock
scope: A stone wave frozen mid-break in the Western Australian outback, near Hyden. T1: a 15 m-high, 110 m-long granite cliff curls over like a giant ocean wave about to crash. T2: the sea never touched it -- the curved 'wave' is a flared slope, hollowed at its base by chemical weathering while it was still buried, then exposed as the soil washed away. T3: the vivid vertical stripes down its face are mineral stains -- iron and carbonate washed down the rock by rain -- painting granite that is roughly 2.6 BILLION years old. (mini: ~3 rungs.)
source: Wikipedia 'Wave Rock'; GeologyInMotion 'Wave Rock'; Explorersweb 'Natural Wonders: Wave Rock'; Yilgarn Craton granite age references (~2.6 Gyr).
framing_note: Voice: lead with the 'frozen wave' image, then the payoff twist -- water shaped it, but underground, not the ocean. Accuracy rail: it's a 'flared slope' shaped by subsurface weathering of ~2.6-Gyr Yilgarn granite; the color streaks are iron/carbonate runoff, not sea spray. Dinner-test payoff: the 'shaped underground, not by waves' rung. Distractors: other inselbergs (note Uluru is sandstone, a good adjacent-but-wrong) keep choices live.
